holding_summary: The Court of Appeals held that a sum entrusted to the decedent for investment was barred by the statute of limitations, and that no promise to pay for shared household expenses could be implied from informal cohabitation absent affirmative proof of an actual agreement.

quotes.text: As in the case of an inn or boarding-house keeper, whoever avails himself of the accommodations furnished by such a person will be held bound as by a promise to pay for them.

in the absence of any relation between the parties, such as inn keeper or hoarding-house keeper, from which said testator could be charged as upon an express promise to pay for his occupancy, no recovery can be had, unless such promise is established by affirmative proof.
As in the case of an inn or boarding-house keeper, whoever avails himself of the accommodations furnished by such a person will be held bound as by a promise to pay for them.

notes: Marked relevant on dictum only: the court affirms, as a general rule, that a genuine innkeeper or boarding-house keeper may recover on an implied promise from an occupant who avails himself of accommodations -- doctrinally favorable to the letting-for-pay practice -- even though it denies recovery on these particular family-cohabitation facts, which were not a real boardinghouse relationship.
